claims.text: A computer network is two or more computing devices connected together so that they can communicate and share data and resources.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Networking a computer lets it share files directly with other users, share hardware such as one printer or one file store instead of many, and have its data backed up and secured centrally rather than machine by machine.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A local area network (LAN) covers one small site such as one building or campus and is owned and managed by the organisation that uses it, whereas a wide area network (WAN) covers a large geographical area and uses long-distance links leased from communication providers.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The internet is the largest example of a WAN: a network of networks that spans the globe, built from countless LANs joined by long-distance links.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: In the client-server model, server computers provide services, files and resources, and client computers request and use them over the network, with the server controlling access.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: In a peer-to-peer model each computer is equal and can act as both client and server, sharing its own files and resources with the others.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A client-server model suits a network where central control, security and backup matter, whereas a peer-to-peer model suits a small network of a few machines that need no server or manager.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A thin client is a computer that depends on a server for its processing and storage: it sends requests and displays results while the server does the work.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A thick client does its own processing and storage locally, running its own applications and keeping its own files, so it needs no server to work.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Thin clients are cheaper to buy and administer and keep data on the server, whereas thick clients cost more but keep working without a server and run demanding applications locally.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A network's topology is the arrangement in which its devices and links are connected together.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: In a bus topology every device connects to one shared backbone cable, and data placed on the cable is seen by every device.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: In a star topology every device connects through its own cable to one central device, and data reaches its destination by passing through that central device.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: In a mesh topology each device is connected to several of the others, so data can travel by more than one route, and a full mesh connects every device to every other device.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A hybrid topology combines two or more of the others, such as stars whose central devices sit on a shared backbone.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A topology's failure behaviour justifies its choice: one broken cable in a star strands one device, whereas a bus backbone fault can stop every device, and a mesh keeps routes open when links fail but costs more links.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Cloud computing provides storage, software and processing as services over the internet, so an organisation uses a provider's infrastructure instead of buying and running its own.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A public cloud is provided for anyone to use, with infrastructure shared among many customers, whereas a private cloud is provided for one organisation, whose infrastructure is not shared with other customers; the words describe who the service is for, not who can read a user's data.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Cloud computing shifts costs from buying hardware to paying for use and lets work happen anywhere with internet access; its drawbacks are dependence on the connection and the provider, and data held on infrastructure the organisation does not own.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Copper cable carries data as electrical signals, which is cheap but open to interference and weakening over distance, whereas fibre-optic cable carries data as pulses of light along glass, which resists interference and carries data further and faster at a higher price.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Wireless connections carry data by radio, so devices can move and no cables are laid, but the signal weakens with distance, is affected by walls, and can be received by others within range.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Microwave links carry data in straight line-of-sight beams between antennas, and satellites relay data between ground stations over very large areas, serving places no cable reaches.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Wired connections are generally faster and more stable but need cable laid to each device, whereas wireless connections are convenient and mobile but their performance varies with distance, walls and interference.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A switch connects devices on a wired LAN and sends each arriving packet only to the port of the device it is addressed to.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A server on a LAN provides the shared services, such as file storage, printing and logon, that a client-server network runs on.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A network interface card (NIC) connects a device to a wired network and carries the device's unique MAC address, which is fixed in the hardware; a wireless NIC (WNIC) does the same by radio, and the device's IP address is assigned by the network it joins.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A wireless access point (WAP) lets wireless devices join the network by radio; a bridge joins two network segments so they behave as one; a repeater takes a weakening signal and re-transmits it stronger so the network reaches further.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A router connects networks together and forwards packets between them, choosing a route for each packet by its destination IP address.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: On the internet, routers pass packets from network to network until a packet reaches the network that holds the destination address, and packets of one message may travel different routes, because each router chooses its own next step.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The unit of data on a network is a packet: a header carrying addresses and a sequence number, and a payload carrying part of the data.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Ethernet is a family of standards for wired LANs that defines the cables and the rules devices follow to place data on the network.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: In CSMA/CD a device listens for a free cable and transmits, keeps listening while it sends, and if two devices transmit together the signals collide, both stop, wait a different random time and try again.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Bit streaming sends multimedia content as a continuous stream of bits, so that playback begins before the whole file has arrived.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Real-time streaming presents an event as it happens, while on-demand streaming starts whenever the user chooses; both depend on the bit rate, and a stream that arrives more slowly than it plays stops to buffer.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The internet is the infrastructure of cables, routers and connected networks, while the World Wide Web is a collection of linked pages of content that runs as a service on that infrastructure.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A modem converts between the digital signals of a computer network and the form the link carries, so a household can reach the internet over a telephone line or a cellular connection.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The PSTN carries data over the ordinary telephone network slowly, a dedicated line is a permanent link reserved for data between two points, and a cell phone network connects devices by radio through masts, giving access wherever coverage reaches.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: An IP address identifies a device on a network so packets can be delivered to it: IPv4 writes it as four denary numbers separated by full stops, and IPv6 as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A public IP address is unique across the internet and reachable from anywhere, whereas a private IP address is used inside a local network and is not unique on the internet.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Subnetting splits one network's address range into smaller networks, which keeps traffic local and makes networks easier to manage.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A URL names a resource on the web in three parts: the scheme, which names how the resource is fetched, the domain name, which names the server that holds it, and the file path, which names the file on that server.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A browser uses a URL by reading the domain name, finding the server's IP address, sending a request for the file at the path, and displaying what returns.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).
